1268.title: The wedding in the code
1268.hook: the four lavan, no dowry, no child marriage
1268.howItsDone: At a Sikh wedding the couple sits before the Guru Granth Sahib; each of the four lavan of Guru Ram Das is read and then sung while the couple walks around the Granth, and Ardas and karah prashad follow.

segments.voice: Yesterday, naam karan: a letter from a hukam, a name chosen from it, and Singh or Kaur. Your line was the name from the hukam.

No exchange of rings at the center of it. No vows written by the couple. No officiant asking if anyone objects. At a Sikh wedding the couple sits side by side on the floor before the Guru Granth Sahib, the groom's scarf in the bride's hand, linking them. A hymn is read. Then it's sung, and as it's sung the couple rises and walks slowly around the Granth, the groom ahead, the bride following, the cloth between them. They sit. Another verse is read, and they walk again. By the end they have circled the Guru, and they're married.
screen: `NO RINGS AT THE CENTER.` → `A SCARF BETWEEN THEM.` → `WALKING AROUND THE GURU.`

segments.voice: Anand Karaj means the ceremony of bliss. Anand is bliss, the same word as the Anand Sahib we heard at the bhog, and karaj is a ceremony or an undertaking. The heart of it is the lavan, a hymn by Guru Ram Das on Ang seven hundred seventy-three of the Guru Granth Sahib, in four stanzas. Each stanza is one lav, one round, read and then sung while the couple walks around the Granth. In paraphrase, the rounds move like a journey: the first is about taking up a life of duty and remembering the Name; the second about losing fear and meeting the Lord in every place; the third about longing and love in the company of the holy; the fourth about peace, the union found. Read that way, the hymn is about the soul and God, and the couple is invited to see their marriage inside that larger love. Now the code. The Sikh Rehat Maryada surrounds the ceremony with rules that protect people. In paraphrase: a marriage should be arranged without regard to caste. No child marriage. No dowry. No consulting the stars for a lucky date or hour. Each removes a way a wedding can become a transaction or a burden, especially for a young bride and her family. What's left is simple: two people, the Guru, a hymn and four rounds.

segments.voice: Bring to mind two people who share a life, newlyweds, your parents, friends who've come through a hard year, and picture them walking slowly together, one step behind the other, the way a couple walks the rounds. Hold them there and wish them steadiness, kindness and peace between them; if you pray, hold them before Waheguru.
Anand Karaj. The Sikh wedding, the ceremony of bliss: the four lavan of Guru Ram Das, sung as the couple walks around the Guru Granth Sahib. Today's word.

1269.title: Remarriage is allowed
1269.hook: the code allows widows and widowers to remarry
1269.howItsDone: The Sikh Rehat Maryada permits a widow or widower to remarry if they wish, and such a marriage is solemnized with the same Anand Karaj ceremony as any other Sikh wedding.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Anand Karaj: Guru Ram Das's lavan, each round walked around the Granth. Your line was four rounds.

She wears white, or pale colors, and has for a long time. At family weddings she helps in the kitchen but keeps to the edge of the courtyard, away from the bride. Nobody says it to her face, but everyone knows what she's supposed to be now: finished. Her husband died, and in the eyes of the people around her, her own life ended with his. In the Punjab the Gurus knew, that was how a widow could be treated. In some places, worse was expected of her. Against that, one short line in the Sikh code reads like a door being unlocked.
screen: `A WIDOW IN WHITE.` → `KEPT TO THE EDGE.` → `A DOOR BEING UNLOCKED.`

segments.voice: The Sikh Rehat Maryada says, in paraphrase: if a woman's husband has died, she may, if she wishes, marry again, to a suitable match. The same holds for a man whose wife has died. And the ceremony is the same Anand Karaj, the same four rounds. Look at the small words. If she wishes: the code doesn't push anyone into a second marriage, and it doesn't forbid one. The choice belongs to the person who is grieving. The same ceremony: no lesser wedding, no back-room version for someone married before. Now the background. The Gurus' world had a custom, sati, in which some widows burned on their husbands' funeral pyres. Guru Amar Das spoke against it. In a salok on Ang seven hundred eighty-seven he says, in paraphrase, that those who burn with their husbands' bodies are not truly satis; true satis are those who live on in virtue and contentment, and who would die of the pain of separation alone. He takes a word that honored burning and gives it to the living. Tradition says he also discouraged the veil and spoke for widows' dignity. The code carries that line forward. A spouse's death is a real ending, and the code doesn't pretend otherwise; Sikhs grieve, and the next lesson is about how. But the survivor is not ended with them. Their life still belongs to them, within the Guru's will, and they are allowed to start again.

segments.voice: Think of someone beginning again, after a death, a divorce, a lost job or an illness, and picture where they are right now. If grief of your own feels like more than you can carry, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach your local emergency help.

1270.title: Funerals in the code
1270.hook: cremation, Kirtan Sohila and Ardas, a reading of the Granth, and no monuments
1270.howItsDone: At a Sikh funeral the body is bathed, dressed and cremated while hymns are sung; Kirtan Sohila and Ardas are recited, a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib follows, and no monument is raised where the body was cremated.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the code's quiet permission: a widow or widower may marry again, if they wish. Your line was starting over allowed.

There's a prayer Sikhs say at night, just before sleep. It's called Kirtan Sohila, it's short, and in some homes children grow up hearing it at bedtime, lights low, the day being put away. Now the same words in a different place. A crematorium, or an open pyre. A family standing close together. The body has been bathed and dressed. And the same bedtime prayer is said over it. The words that close an ordinary day are the words that close a life.
screen: `A PRAYER BEFORE SLEEP.` → `THE SAME WORDS AT THE PYRE.` → `CLOSING A DAY, CLOSING A LIFE.`

segments.voice: The Sikh Rehat Maryada lays out a funeral in a few plain steps. In paraphrase: the body is bathed and clothed, and if the person was initiated, the five articles of faith stay with them. The body is cremated; where cremation isn't possible, the code allows other means. On the way and at the pyre, hymns are sung, Kirtan Sohila is recited when the fire is lit, and Ardas is said. Then a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib begins, at home or in a gurdwara, and when it's complete there's a bhog, the closing we met not long ago. Notice what the code leaves out. It discourages loud wailing and breast-beating, and rejects rituals that grew up around death outside the Guru's teaching. It asks that no monument be built where the body was cremated. Why so plain? In Sikh teaching a death happens within the hukam, God's order, the same order that gave the life. Grief is real, and the Gurus wrote about it; but the goodbye turns the family toward the Word instead of a stone. The ashes aren't enshrined. The reading of the Granth is the memorial. That's why Kirtan Sohila fits: the prayer of going to rest, of a day returned to the One who gave it. Said at the pyre, it meets death as the last evening, with the same words as every other. A simple goodbye isn't a cold one. Nothing stands between the mourners and the Guru.
screen: `BATHED, CLOTHED, CREMATED.` · `KIRTAN SOHILA AND ARDAS.` · `A READING OF THE GRANTH, NO MONUMENT.` · `A DEATH WITHIN THE HUKAM.` · then, large: `SIMPLE GOODBYES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has died, or someone you've had to let go of, and without reliving the whole story, ask what few plain words would be enough for a goodbye: a single line, maybe only their name, said once. Hold those words, or say Waheguru once for them if you pray, and if the memory gets heavy, it's fine to stop and simply breathe. If grief ever turns toward hurting yourself, please reach out now: call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

1271.title: The Guru Panth
1271.hook: the collective Khalsa carries the Guru's authority with the Granth
1271.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of Guru Granth and Guru Panth together; on questions bearing on the Gurus' teaching, a gathering of the Panth may pass a gurmata, a resolution made in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib and in keeping with Gurbani.

segments.voice: Yesterday, funerals in the code: Kirtan Sohila at the pyre, a reading of the Granth, no monument. Your line was simple goodbyes.

A question has split the community. Should it do this, or that? Nobody is sure, and opinions are loud. So people gather, the Guru Granth Sahib open at the front. They talk it through, not in a back office but before the Granth. Ardas is said. A decision is reached together, and announced as something more than a vote. In Sikh life, a decision made by the gathered Khalsa in the Guru's presence can carry the Guru's weight. How can ordinary people hold that? Sikhs answer with two words.
screen: `A QUESTION SPLITS THE SANGAT.` → `DECIDED BEFORE THE GRANTH.` → `MORE THAN A VOTE.`

segments.voice: Panth means a path, and so the people who walk it together. Guru Panth is the Khalsa community as Guru. Tradition says that before Guru Gobind Singh died, he ended the line of human Gurus and placed the Guru in two forms: the Guru Granth Sahib, the Word, and the Guru Panth, the community of the Khalsa. Sikhs speak of them together: Guru Granth, Guru Panth. The Granth holds the teaching; the Panth carries it out, decides together, and acts. Neither stands alone. A Panth that ignored the Granth would be a crowd with opinions; a Granth with no Panth would be a book no one lives. The Sikh Rehat Maryada gives this a working form. In paraphrase: a gurmata, a resolution made with the Guru's assent, is passed by a gathering of the Panth in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib, on questions that bear on the Gurus' teaching. A gurmata can't overrule Gurbani; it applies it. One story Sikhs tell shows the idea in a single scene. When the Tenth Guru founded the Khalsa, he initiated the first Five, and then, tradition says, asked them to initiate him. The Guru stood before his own disciples to receive what he had just given. The teacher put himself inside the community he had made. That's the Guru Panth in a picture: authority living not in one person at the top but in the gathered people, bowed before the Word.

1272.title: Who gives amrit
1272.hook: five amritdhari Sikhs, with a sixth attending the Granth
1272.howItsDone: Under the Sikh Rehat Maryada, amrit is given in a quiet place in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib by five amritdhari Sikhs who keep the code, while a sixth Sikh attends the Granth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Guru Panth: the gathered Khalsa, carrying the Guru's authority beside the Granth. Your line was the people as guru.

A door is closed. Not locked, just closed, so the room stays quiet. Inside, the Guru Granth Sahib rests open, and one Sikh sits beside it. Five more stand together, wearing the five Ks, washed and ready. Six people and the book. That's the whole staff. Nobody arrives from a head office; nobody signs a certificate for an institution. Yesterday's big idea, the Guru Panth, shrinks here to the size of one room, on the day someone new is about to join. So who gives amrit?
screen: `A CLOSED DOOR, A QUIET ROOM.` → `SIX PEOPLE AND THE BOOK.` → `WHO GIVES AMRIT?`

segments.voice: The Sikh Rehat Maryada answers plainly. In paraphrase: the initiation may be held in any quiet, suitable place. Besides the Guru Granth Sahib, six Sikhs need to be present. One attends the Granth. Five give the amrit. Start with the one. Their task is to sit in attendance on the Guru Granth Sahib, which Sikhs honor as the Guru present in the room. The ceremony doesn't happen while the book waits on a shelf; it happens in the Guru's presence, with someone caring for that presence the whole time. Then the five. The code asks that they be Sikhs who have taken amrit themselves, who keep the five Ks, and who live by the code. You can only pass on what you have received. Nobody gives amrit on the strength of a title, a degree or a family name; the five give it because they already stand inside the promise they're about to offer. Now the number. The code asks for five, not one. Together they stand in for the panj pyare, the five beloved ones of Anandpur, whom this path met long ago. So the authority in the room doesn't belong to any one of them; it sits between them. And the five aren't a fixed set of people. Any five who meet the code's terms can be chosen for the day. Another month, another town, five different Sikhs, and the amrit is the same amrit. So the answer isn't a single who. It's a five.

1273.title: The instructions after amrit
1273.hook: the initiated are told the banis, the five Ks and the four things to avoid
1273.howItsDone: After amrit is given, one of the five explains the rehat to the newly initiated: their new spiritual family, the daily banis, the five Ks and the four kurahits to avoid, as the Sikh Rehat Maryada lays out.

segments.voice: Yesterday, who gives amrit: five who have taken it themselves, and a sixth beside the Granth. Your line was the five give.

The amrit has been drunk. It has been sprinkled on the eyes and the hair. The words have been called out and answered. From the outside, this looks like the end. And still nobody leaves. One of the five turns to the newly initiated and starts to speak, slowly, the way you'd give directions to someone who has to remember them without a map. Before anyone walks out of that quiet room, the promise gets spelled out, piece by piece, out loud. Nothing is left in small print.
screen: `THE AMRIT HAS BEEN GIVEN.` → `AND STILL NOBODY LEAVES.` → `THE PROMISE, SPELLED OUT.`

segments.voice: The Sikh Rehat Maryada sets out what is said. In paraphrase, four parts. First, a new family. The initiated are told that from today they're born into the Guru's household: Guru Gobind Singh their spiritual father, Mata Sahib Kaur their spiritual mother, Anandpur their home. Whatever caste or clan they came from is left behind; they are one family with every Sikh of the Khalsa. Second, the daily banis, morning, evening and night, prayers this path walked through not long ago: Japji and Jaap among them at dawn, Rehras at evening, Kirtan Sohila before sleep. Third, the five Ks: kesh, uncut hair; kangha, the comb; kara, the steel bracelet; kachhera, the shorts worn underneath; and kirpan, the sword. Each is kept on the body. Fourth, the things to avoid. The code calls them kurahits and names four: dishonoring the hair by cutting it; eating the meat of an animal killed in the ritual way the code calls kutha; sexual contact with anyone other than one's spouse; and using tobacco. Someone who commits one must come back and take amrit again. Look at the order. Family comes first: who you belong to, then what you do. The rules hang on the relationship, not the other way round. And it's all said aloud, in the Guru's presence, before the five, so nobody can say later they weren't told. These are the promises of those who take amrit; as this path said long ago, there are many ways of being Sikh, and every seeker is welcome.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one promise you've already made, to a person, to yourself, or to God if you pray, and find the plain words for it, short enough to fit on a sticky note. Say it once in your head, slowly, as if someone were listening for every word, and notice whether the plain version feels heavier or lighter than the vague one.
The instructions after amrit. The new Khalsa family, the daily banis, the five Ks and the four things to avoid, spoken aloud before anyone leaves. Today's word.
Your line: what is promised. Not a vague feeling, but words that are specific, spoken and heard. Until tomorrow.

1274.title: When rehat is broken
1274.hook: breaking the code is met with a penance set by five Sikhs
1274.howItsDone: Under the Sikh Rehat Maryada, a Sikh who has broken the code confesses before the sangat in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib, five Sikhs set a tankhah, and the matter closes with an ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the instructions after amrit: a new family, the banis, the five Ks, the things to avoid. Your line was what is promised.

This week has been full of words said out loud: four rounds at a wedding, a prayer at the pyre, five Sikhs giving amrit, the rehat explained before anyone leaves. Which leaves the question nobody likes to ask at a ceremony. What happens when someone breaks it? Not dramatically. A person who promised, and meant it, slips. A rule bends, then gives. In some everyday groups, an office, a team, a family, that's handled with silence: the person drifts to the back row, then out the door. The Sikh code takes a different road. It walks the person to the front.
screen: `A WEEK OF WORDS SAID ALOUD.` → `WHAT IF ONE IS BROKEN?` → `THE CODE WALKS YOU TO THE FRONT.`

segments.voice: Tankhah is the penance set for a Sikh who has broken the code; someone under it is called a tankhaiya. Here's the process in the Sikh Rehat Maryada, paraphrased. The person goes to the nearest sangat, the gathered congregation, and stands before it in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib. There they say what they did; no one has to drag it out of them, because the code expects the person to come. Then five Sikhs, chosen from the sangat and in good standing under the code, hear the case and decide the tankhah. The person accepts it without arguing back, and the matter closes with an ardas, the standing prayer, offered for them. Look at what that does. First, the confession is open: owned in front of the community the promise was made to, not whispered behind a curtain. Second, the judgment is shared. Not one elder with a grudge or a soft spot, but five, the same number that gives amrit. Welcomed in by five, set right by five. Third, there's an end. The tankhah is set, carried out and prayed over, and the person stands again as one of the sangat; the code doesn't leave a mark on them for life. For the gravest breaches, the four named yesterday, the person also takes amrit again after penance. For other lapses, the tankhah itself is the road back. What the process never offers is hiding. The way home goes through the front of the room.
screen: `TANKHAH: THE PENANCE FOR A BREACH.` · `CONFESSED BEFORE THE SANGAT.` · `FIVE SIKHS SET THE PENANCE.` · `AN ARDAS, AND IT IS CLOSED.` · then, large: `OWN IT.`

segments.voice: Let one small, recent mistake come to mind, not the biggest, and say it to yourself in one plain sentence that starts with I: not they made me, not it happened, but I did this. Then add one more sentence, what would set it right, and let the two sit side by side.
Tankhah. The penance set for a Sikh who has broken the code, decided by five Sikhs before the sangat and closed with an ardas. Today's word.
Your line: own it. Welcomed in by five, and set right by five. That's a week of promises.
